strengths: The paper is technically sound: the core result (Prop. 2) — transferring output-space unsafe-set constraints back to the input space through shared zonotope generator factors — is correct, with complete proofs provided in the appendix, including Corollary 1 establishing the refinement is lossless for both verification and falsification.

A complete verification/falsification system (Alg. 1) is built that integrates the refinement into a branch-and-bound procedure, and the implementation uses only matrix operations enabling full GPU acceleration and batched verification of subproblems — a practical engineering contribution.

The evaluation is reasonably strong: comparisons against the top-5 tools of VNN-COMP'24 on 7 standardized benchmarks, plus ablation studies covering (i) falsification strategies, (ii) refinement variants (none/network-wise/layer-wise), and (iii) GPU acceleration and batch size. The refinement demonstrably reduces subproblem counts (e.g., 24785.6 → 1024.3 on acasxu prop_3), and the tool achieves results that would rank in the top 5 of the competition.
The proposed set-based falsification (boundary-point transfer via shared factors) outperforms center-based and FGSM attacks in their ablation (Table 3).

The 'shadow'/latent-space view of constrained zonotope propagation (all propagated sets as projections of the same constrained hypercube) is a clean framing that nicely unifies input refinement, ReLU splitting, and counterexample extraction; illustrations (Figs. 1-3) aid understanding.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the core observation that propagated zonotopes share the same generator factors β (so constraints in the output space induce constraints in the input space) is a fairly straightforward algebraic fact, and the authors themselves cite closely related work exploiting 'dependencies between propagated zonotopes' (ref. [24], HSCC 2020). The 'latent space' terminology somewhat overclaims novelty — no learning or nontrivial latent structure is involved beyond standard zonotope parameterization; the paper is best viewed as an application of known dependency structure to input-set refinement.

The reported results are competitive but consistently below α-β-CROWN on most benchmarks (e.g., 98.9% vs 100% on acasxu; 80.0% vs 87.8% on cora; 84.3% vs 100% on safenlp), so the system does not advance the state of the art on overall solve rates; the headline claim is only 'would place in the top 5', and the tool did not actually participate in VNN-COMP'24.

Comparison methodology concerns: results are compared against competition-reported numbers obtained under the competition's hardware and timeout settings, while the proposed tool runs on a different, powerful setup (2×AMD EPYC, 2TB RAM, NVIDIA A100 40GB GPU, with per-instance memory-reduced batch size halving) — this makes both time comparisons and possibly solve-rate comparisons under timeouts less rigorous. No wall-clock or timeout configuration equivalence analysis is provided.

The falsification component is weak in absolute terms: the set-based attack falsifies only 621/1080 instances (57.5%) on safenlp, and the boundary-point heuristic along normal vectors of the specification is quite limited compared to modern gradient/optimization-based attacks; no comparison against stronger attacks (e.g., Carlini-Wagner [10]) is given.

Several methodological details are underspecified: how refinement and splitting constraints are combined and selected across iterations, how many refinement iterations are performed per branch-and-bound node, whether refinement is applied to child sets recursively, and how the approximated constrained-zonotope bounds (Prop. 3, iterated) affect completeness and accuracy of the verification check (Eq. 8 uses these approximated bounds). Soundness of the overall pipeline depends on this approximation but its impact is not quantified.

No statement about releasing code or an artifact; a MATLAB/CORA implementation with custom tricks (Appendix B) raises reproducibility concerns for a paper whose central claims rest on benchmark performance.

The writing contains numerous typos and grammatical issues ('activiation', 'formluate', 'algroithm', 'therefor', 'an counterexample'), which detract from polish; the 'layer-wise' vs 'network-wise' refinement distinction is described only informally without a formal definition or algorithm.

Theoretical analysis is thin: there is no discussion of convergence of the iterative refinement, growth of the constraint set size over iterations, or complexity of maintaining constrained zonotope representations in a deep network (generator counts grow with layers, and the C matrices grow with specifications × generators).

strengths: The core technical observation is clean and correctly formalized: zonotope propagation leaves the underlying hypercube (the 'latent space') unchanged, which enables transferring output specifications back to the input space as linear constraints on the generator factors (Prop. 2), and the proofs in Appendix C are essentially sound.

The proposed iterative input refinement is sound and complete in combination with branch-and-bound (Cor. 1), and the set-based falsification step preserves correctness since candidate counterexamples are explicitly verified.
The implementation uses only matrix operations, enabling GPU batching of subproblems; the ablation (Tab. 2b) convincingly demonstrates the speed-up from GPU acceleration and batch size.

The evaluation on standardized VNN-COMP'24 benchmarks against the top-5 competition tools is transparent and reproducible in spirit, and the ablations (refinement strategy, falsification method, GPU/batch size) support the design choices.
Well-organized presentation with helpful illustrative examples (Fig. 2, Fig. 3) and a clear algorithm description.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the central idea reduces to back-propagating specification constraints through zonotope generators, a fairly straightforward algebraic manipulation (Prop. 2). The 'latent space' framing largely repackages the well-known fact that zonotopes propagated through affine maps share the same generator factors; the authors themselves point to closely related dependency-utilization work [24] and constrained zonotopes [33]. The contribution feels incremental over these lines of work.

The empirical results do not demonstrate superiority over the state of the art: α-β-CROWN and NeuralSAT outperform the proposed method on most benchmarks (e.g., cora, metaroom, safenlp), and the claim of being 'among the top-ranking tools' is overstated relative to what Table 1 shows.

The evaluation is incomplete and not hardware-fair: only 7 of the VNN-COMP'24 benchmarks are used, baseline numbers are imported from the competition report rather than re-run under identical conditions (hardware, timeout, GPU access), and the timeout setting is not clearly stated. The choice of benchmarks is not justified.

Ablations are narrow: input refinement is ablated only on acasxu, falsification only on safenlp; the effect of the refinement on end-to-end runtime (not just subproblem count) across benchmarks is not reported, so the claimed speed-up mechanism is not fully validated.

Comparison baselines are missing for the headline claim: GPU-accelerated matrix-based verification exists in prior systems (e.g., the massively parallel approach of [39], GPU support in α-β-CROWN), but the paper does not empirically isolate the benefit of its approach versus these design choices under equal settings.

The falsification heuristic (Eq. 9) is simplistic (boundary point along a normal vector) and is shown to be better only against weak alternatives (center, FGSM); no comparison with stronger optimization-based attacks [10].

Presentation issues undermine polish: multiple typos ('activiation', 'formluate', 'Therefor', 'algroithm', 'an counterexample'), a typo in the Cor. 1 proof (subset relation written as unsafe set instead of safe inputs), and the equivalence claimed in Cor. 1 is argued loosely.

The latent space does not strictly remain fixed once constraints/splits are introduced (constrained hypercube changes), so the motivating narrative is somewhat inaccurate as stated and could mislead readers about what is technically new.

strengths: The core idea is elegant and technically sound: interpreting zonotope propagation as projections ('shadows') of a shared high-dimensional hypercube gives a clean way to back-propagate output specifications onto the shared generator factors, enabling specification-driven input refinement (Prop. 2) with a correct proof in the appendix.

The refinement is integrated into a complete branch-and-bound procedure with both verification and falsification, and the abstraction-refinement loop is provably sound (Corollary 1, Prop. 3 over-approximation of constrained-zonotope bounds avoids LPs and is GPU-friendly).

The implementation using only matrix operations enables genuine GPU batching of subproblems, which is a practical advantage over many existing verifiers; the CPU/GPU and batch-size ablations (Tab. 2b) directly support this claim.

Evaluation against the top-5 tools of VNN-COMP'24 on standardized benchmarks is a meaningful, externally calibrated comparison, and the ablations (refinement type, falsification method) justify the main design choices.
The paper is generally well organized, with a clear motivating example (Ex. 1, Figs. 1-3) that makes the latent-space view easy to follow.
weaknesses: Novelty is more limited than the framing suggests: the key mechanism — exploiting dependencies between propagated zonotope generators to obtain subsets of reachable sets — is essentially the contribution of [24] (Kochdumper et al., HSCC 2020), and constrained zonotopes are from [33]. The 'latent space' terminology mostly renames existing zonotope-generator structure; the genuinely new parts (specification-driven input refinement inside branch-and-bound, GPU batching) are incremental.

The tool does not actually outperform state of the art: in Tab. 1 it is below alpha-beta-CROWN on nearly all benchmarks and below NeuralSAT on 4 of 7 (e.g., cora 80.0% vs 87.8%, safenlp 84.3% vs 100.0%). The 'top-5' claim is honest but modest; the contribution would be stronger if the refinement were shown to close or invert these gaps.

Fairness of the comparison is unclear: the tool runs on an A100 GPU with large batch sizes on a 128-thread machine, while the VNN-COMP'24 baseline numbers were obtained under competition conditions; a time- and hardware-normalized comparison (or at least a discussion) is missing. Also, only 7 benchmarks are selected without strong justification.

The falsification method is compared only against FGSM and a trivial center-point attack (Tab. 3); stronger optimization-based attacks (e.g., PGD, Carlini-Wagner) are cited but not compared, leaving the falsification advantage under-supported.

Corollary 1 is stated incorrectly: 'Phi(X|C<=d) ∩ U = ∅ ⟺ Phi(X) ∩ U = ∅' is false as written (verification of the refined set alone does not verify the full set); the proof correctly shows a conjunction with the complement being safe, but the formal statement is sloppy.

Several practical details that affect reproducibility are thin: no statement about releasing code, the split heuristic ('largest-most sensitive input dimension, split at middle') is described only in the appendix and is simple, and there is no comparison to stronger splitting heuristics despite a rich related-work list.

Writing quality issues: multiple typos ('activiation', 'formluate', 'Therefor', 'algroithm', 'an counterexample'), and the latent-space narrative is somewhat over-marketed relative to the technical substance.

strengths: The core idea of exploiting the shared generator/factor space ('latent space') of projection-based set representations to transfer output specifications back to the input set is elegant, clearly formalized (Prop. 2), and comes with a soundness proof (Prop. 2 and Corollary 1 in the appendix).

Integration of the refinement into a branch-and-bound procedure with GPU-friendly, matrix-only implementation is a practically valuable contribution; the reported speed-ups (82.8% on acasxu, 89.8% on safenlp) and subproblem reductions (59.6%/65.3%) are substantial.

Evaluation against the top-5 tools of VNN-COMP'24 on standardized, competitive benchmarks is a strong, transparent comparison; matching top performance on 4 of 8 benchmarks on inferior hardware (laptop vs. server GPU) is impressive.

Extensive ablation studies (refinement on/off, GPU vs. CPU and batch size, falsification method vs. FGSM, splitting heuristics, exact vs. approximated bounds) provide good justification of design choices, and limitations are honestly reported (e.g., overhead on low-dimensional benchmarks).
The paper is well written with helpful illustrative examples (Fig. 2, Fig. 3) and a clean notation section; computational complexity is analyzed (Prop. 4).
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is moderate: the 'latent space' is essentially the well-known fact that all sets propagated through a network share the same zonotope generators, and constraint back-transfer is closely related to backward reachability and existing dependency-based zonotope techniques (Kochdumper et al., 2020) as well as preimage enclosure work (Kotha et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2024). The framing risks overselling a standard observation under a new name.

The tool does not clearly beat the strongest baseline (α-β-CROWN), which achieves 100% on safenlp vs. 89.2% and better results on acasxu, cora, and meta-room; 'competitive performance' is fair but the contribution does not establish a new state of the art.

Key ablation results (refinement, splitting heuristics, GPU speed-up) are only reported in detail for two benchmarks (acasxu, safenlp); the behavior and overhead of refinement on the other six benchmarks are relegated to a qualitative discussion, and refinement actually increases total runtime on tllverifybench (18.7s to 36.1s).

Comparison against VNN-COMP'24 results is conducted on different hardware (laptop with RTX 4070 vs. A10G servers); while %solved under a fixed timeout is comparable, timing-based claims of efficiency relative to the competition tools are not apples-to-apples.

Only 8 of the VNN-COMP benchmarks are used, and the selection criteria for these 8 (beyond being 'competitive and standardized') are not fully justified, raising concerns about benchmark cherry-picking.

Several technical details are under-specified: Algorithm 1's falsification step (line 10) reuses the counter 'i' ambiguously as both subproblem counter and constraint index, and the splitting heuristic (Appendix B) is only validated against one local-gradient baseline.

There is little theoretical analysis of the refinement's tightness or convergence; the backward transfer uses |·|1 bounding of the error generators, whose conservatism growth across iterations and layers is not characterized, and no guarantee is given on how quickly the intersection with the unsafe set shrinks.

Implementation in MATLAB/CORA may limit reproducibility and adoption compared to the Python-based tooling ecosystem of the competing verifiers, although release of the code is not explicitly promised.

strengths: The paper is technically sound: the core refinement (Prop. 2) is correct, and a full proof plus a soundness corollary for verification/falsification is provided in the appendix.

The evaluation on standardized VNN-COMP'24 benchmarks against the top-5 competition tools is appropriate, and the tool matches top performance on 4 of 8 benchmarks despite running on weaker hardware than the competition.

The ablation studies are unusually thorough for this area: input refinement on/off (Tab. 2, 5), GPU vs. CPU and batch size (Tab. 3a), falsification vs. FGSM (Tab. 3b), splitting heuristics (Tab. 4), and fast vs. exact constrained-zonotope bounds (Tab. 6).

The pure matrix-operation implementation with batched GPU computation is a practical contribution, and the fast Fourier-Motzkin-inspired bound approximation (Prop. 3) is a useful engineering trick justified empirically.
The paper is well-written and largely reproducible (CORA/MATLAB implementation, public benchmark suite, hyperparameters disclosed).
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the 'latent space' framing largely rebrands the well-known fact that zonotope generators are shared across propagated sets. The core idea of exploiting generator dependencies to obtain subsets of reachable sets already exists (Kochdumper et al., 2020, cited by the authors), and back-propagating output constraints to the input is closely related to standard backward linear-relaxation/CROWN-style bound propagation. Prop. 2 itself is a straightforward |.|1 relaxation of a linear inequality.

The refinement is sound but crude: bounding the non-input generators via the |.|1 relaxation can produce very loose input constraints, and the procedure may not converge; the paper does not analyze contraction rate or provide any theoretical guarantee on the number of iterations needed.

The tool does not outperform the state of the art: it trails alpha-beta-CROWN on acasxu (99.5% vs. 100%), cora (81.1% vs. 87.8%), meta-room (97.0% vs. 98.0%), and safenlp (89.2% vs. 100%), so the central claim reduces to 'competitive' rather than advancing the frontier.

Comparison fairness is questionable: results are compared against VNN-COMP'24 runs on different hardware (competition A10G servers vs. the authors' laptop GPU), with the authors' own timeout settings and only 8 of the competition benchmarks selected; a head-to-head re-run of competing tools on identical hardware is missing.

Several design choices appear hand-tuned and under-justified (8 refinement iterations, 4 bounding iterations per refinement, the enclosure-gradient heuristic), and the complexity of the refinement per iteration grows with the number of generators (O(kappa q^3 + xi p q^2)), which could hinder scaling though no scaling analysis is given.

The falsification step is weak: a single candidate counterexample per unsafe-set constraint row generated via a sign heuristic (Eq. 9), with no multi-start or optimization, and its comparison is only against FGSM rather than stronger attacks (PGD, C&W).

Presentation issues remain despite LLM-assisted editing: typos ('formluate', 'heurtistic', 'along at center'), a potentially confusing indexing in Alg. 1 line 10 (beta-tilde_i vs. beta-tilde([q0])), and the abstract's 'latent space' terminology may mislead readers familiar with learned latent spaces.

strengths: The core idea is clean and well-motivated: exploiting the shared generator variables (the 'latent space') between the input zonotope and the output enclosure to transfer output specifications backwards and iteratively enclose the preimage of unsafe outputs. This is an elegant use of a standard but underexploited structural property of projection-based set representations.

The technical presentation is careful and rigorous: Prop. 2 and its proof (Appendix F) plus Corollary 1 establish soundness of the refinement for both verification and falsification, and the soundness argument correctly handles the subtlety that the refined set over-approximates the unsafe inputs rather than preserving the full output enclosure.

The evaluation is substantial and follows accepted community practice: comparison against the top-5 tools from VNN-COMP'24 on 8 standardized benchmarks, with the tool matching top performance on several benchmarks (collins-rul-cnn, dist-shift, linearizenn, tllverifybench) despite running on inferior hardware.

The ablation studies are unusually thorough and genuinely informative: input refinement reduces subproblems by ~60-65% on acasxu/safenlp and improves %Solved on cora (40% -> 81.1%) and safenlp (80.8% -> 89.2%); the appendix honestly reports cases where refinement hurts (acasxu, linearizenn, tllverifybench per-iteration overhead) and quantifies the trade-off between exact and approximated constrained-zonotope bounds (Tab. 6).

The GPU/batch-wise implementation using only matrix operations is a practical contribution, with a demonstrated 80-90% speedup, and the enclosure-gradient splitting heuristic (Appendix B) is a sensible, evaluated addition.

The paper is transparent: hardware discrepancies are disclosed, the falsification method is compared against a known baseline (FGSM), computational complexity is analyzed (Prop. 4), and LLM usage is disclosed.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate rather than groundbreaking. The 'latent space' is essentially the well-known fact that a zonotope is an affine image of a hypercube, and transferring output constraints to generator space is closely related to existing work the authors themselves cite: Kochdumper et al. (2020) on 'utilizing dependencies to obtain subsets of reachable sets', and preimage enclosure via linear bounding (Kotha et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2024). The contribution is a sensible recombination and systematization rather than a fundamentally new technique.

The headline comparison is against numbers reported in the VNN-COMP'24 proceedings rather than re-running all baselines on identical hardware, which weakens the comparison despite the hardware disclosure. The tool also does not reach state of the art on several benchmarks (safenlp: 89.2% vs. 100.0% for alpha-beta-CROWN; cora: 81.1% vs. 87.8%), so 'competitive performance' is accurate but the tool is not clearly superior anywhere.

The iterative refinement adds non-trivial per-iteration overhead that can dominate on low-dimensional benchmarks (tllverifybench: avg. time nearly doubles from 18.7s to 36.1s; acasxu and linearizenn also slow down), meaning the method's applicability is concentrated on high-dimensional input spaces. A more adaptive termination criterion is not explored beyond a fixed iteration count.
MATLAB/CORA implementation may limit adoption and reproducibility relative to the Python-based ecosystems of the main competitors; no code release or artifact is explicitly stated in the manuscript.

The falsification baseline comparison is limited: FGSM is a weak, older attack; comparison against stronger optimization-based attacks (e.g., C&W) or the adversarial machinery inside alpha-beta-CROWN would be more convincing.

Some presentation issues: a few typos ('formluate', 'Splitting heuristics' appendix phrasing), and the paper would benefit from a clearer discussion of how refinement interacts with the queue-based branch-and-bound ordering (e.g., whether refinement can starve falsification in pathological cases).
